summary.value: This paper introduces Adversarially Trained Process Reward Models (APRM). The core idea involves a two-player, general-sum game where a Generator learns to generate reasoning errors to deceive a PRM, which concurrently learns to detect them. Experimental results show that APRM improves solver accuracy on mathematical reasoning benchmarks compared to baseline methods.

strengths.value:
1. The paper investigates an important and timely topic.
2. The method is supported by theoretical analysis.
3. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method.

weaknesses.value:
1. The paper fails to cite and compare with [1], which also explores adversarial training for reward models. This omission makes it difficult to assess the precise novelty of this work relative to existing approaches.

2. The evaluation is limited to using the PRM for inference-time supervision. It remains unclear whether the APRM can perform effectively as a reward signal in an RL post-training setup, which is a critical and common application for reward models.

I am open to raising my score if these points are addressed.

[1] Adversarial Training of Reward Models (COLM 2025)

questions.value: Please refer to the Weaknesses section above.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission9885 by Reviewer jiVq

comment.value:
Dear Reviewer jiVq, 

Thank you for the thoughtful and constructive review. We appreciate the recognition of our contributions and the opportunity to address the points raised.

> W1: The paper fails to cite and compare with [1], which also explores adversarial training for reward models. This omission makes it difficult to assess the precise novelty of this work relative to existing approaches. 

We thank the reviewer for highlighting [1]. We have added [1] to related works and as a baseline in the paper. Below, we clarify (a) how [1] differs from our setting, and (b) a direct empirical comparison.

(a) _Methodological Differences:_ 

* While [1] proposes adversarial training for _outcome reward models_, it does not address _process reward modeling_. In [1], adversarial samples are identified by the disagreement between two pretrained outcome RMs for the same full response. The generator is trained only to produce samples with low inter-RM agreement, and after this stage it is used as a static generator to curate data for training a new RM.

* In contrast, APRM trains a _process-reward model_ with an actively evolving generator that is updated in tandem with the PRM. This yields progressively harder, fine-grained reasoning errors that static generators cannot easily provide.

* The authors of [1] report that (i) training the generator for more than two rounds leads to diminishing returns, and (ii) if the two outcome RMs share blind spots—assigning similar high scores to the same incorrect responses—the disagreement-based signal fails entirely. 

(b) _Empirical Comparison_:

To ensure a fair comparison, we trained a _process reward model_ using [1]’s methodology (denoted **ARM**). Following [1], we: 
- train two PRMs using PRM800K [2], a human-labelled process level supervision dataset for math
- train a generator (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) to generate steps with low agreement between these PRMs, and
- trained a final PRM using this static generator.

The performance of ARM versus APRM is shown below:

| Method        | MATH500 | JEEBench | OlympiadB | AIME25 | AMC  |
|--------------|--------:|-----:|----------:|-------:|-----:|
| ||**GPT-OSS-120B** |        |      |                 |
| ARM          | 89.2    | 62.4 | 77.6      | 87.9   | 63.3 |
| **APRM (Ours)**  | **91.4**    | **70.3** | **89.4**      | **94.5**   | **70.7** |
| ||**Gemma-3-27B**  |                |        |      |
| ARM          | 86.0    | 51.0 | 61.0      | 71.4   | 30.0 |
| **APRM (Ours)**  | **91.4**    | **74.4** | **90.7**      | **91.9**   | **60.8** |

APRM substantially outperforms ARM: **+7.2** pp on GPT-OSS-120B and **+22.0** pp on Gemma-3-27B, demonstrating that static generator is considerably less effective than a dynamically evolving generator for process-reward model training.

---

> W2: The evaluation is limited to using the PRM for inference-time supervision. It remains unclear whether the APRM can perform effectively as a reward signal in an RL post-training setup, which is a critical and common application for reward models.

We thank you for suggesting this experiment. To address this concern, we train a solver LLM using the APRM-trained PRM as a dense reward signal for RL post-training. 

Due to compute constraints, we perform LoRA fine-tuning on Gemma-3-12B and compare three reward setups:

1.	Final Correct — standard outcome-based RL using only final answer correctness.

2.	ReST-MCTS PRM — dense rewards from a PRM trained via ReST-MCTS.

3.	APRM PRM (Ours) — dense rewards from our adversarially trained PRM.

All models are finetuned on the MATH training split.

| Method          | MATH500 | JEEB  | OlympiadB | AIME25 | AMC  |
|-----------------|--------:|------:|----------:|-------:|-----:|
| Base Model (CoT)            |   76.8  |  43.2 |     35.6  |   53.0 | 23.3 |
| Final Correct   |   80.0  |  48.2 |     40.0  |   59.8 | 21.0 |
| ReST-MCTS PRM   |   83.0  |  51.6 |     43.2  |   61.4 | 23.3 |
| **APRM (Ours)** | **86.8**|**58.6**| **48.0**  |**65.7**|**25.3**|

We find that, APRM provides a much stronger RL reward signal, outperforming both outcome-based RL and ReST-MCTS PRMs.
It improves over final-answer supervision by **+6.8** pp (MATH500), **+10.4** pp (JEEB), and **+10.9** pp (AIME25).

This demonstrates that APRM-trained PRMs are reliable dense reward functions for RL post-training, not just inference-time supervisors.

---

We thank you again for the thoughtful review. We believe we have addressed all your concerns, and if anything remains unclear, we would be happy to clarify. 

We look forward to your response.

References

[1] Adversarial Training of Reward Models (COLM 2025)

[2] Let's Verify Step by Step (ICLR 2024)

Dear Reviewer, 

Thank you for your continued engagement. We appreciate that you are open to increasing your score.

We have updated the manuscript's **Appendix 6.14 (Training Details)**, to include the hyperparameters for both the ARM baseline and the RL post-training experiments.

The key configurations we used are:

1. **ARM Baseline** 

 - *Backbone*: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (for the PRMs and Generator).
 - *Outcome RM Training*: We trained two PRMs on PRM800K dataset (using the Bradley Terry model and different seeds). We could not use the exact training data as in the paper, because the paper originally trains an outcome reward model but we train a process reward model.
    - *Optimization*: AdamW, Learning Rate $1 \times 10^{-6}$, Batch Size 64, 1 Epoch.
 - *Generator Training*: We use RLOO, as mentioned in the paper, to train the generator. Trained using LR $5 \times 10^{-7}$, Batch Size 64, generating 16 samples per prompt using AdamW optimizer.
 - *Final PRM Training*: We generated 16 samples per prompt. For this set of 16 prompts, we calculate the score from the current PRM version and filter the completions with score less than average score for that prompt. We then do variance based filtering with z >1.96. 

2. **RL Post-Training (Using Trained PRMs for RL)**

 - *Model*: Gemma-3-12B supervised by the trained PRMs in addition to final correctness reward.
 - *Algorithm*: GRPO
    - *LoRA Config*: Rank $r=8$, Alpha $\alpha=16$. 
    - *Target modules*: All linear layers.
- Hyperparameters:
    - *LR*: $5 \times 10^{-7}$ (AdamW)
    - *Group Size*: 16
    - *KL $\beta$*:  0.01
    - *Clip Ratio*: $\epsilon = 0.2$
 - *Reward Formulation*: Since the starting point for GRPO should be the same within the group, we calculated the reward as the sum of the PRM probabilities across all reasoning steps.

We have also updated the **Related Work** section to include ARM baseline. We hope these details address your remaining concerns regarding the reliability of the new results.

We would be happy to clarify further if anything remains. 

Thanks,

Authors

summary.value: This paper introduces Adversarially Trained Process Reward Models (APRM), a novel framework for training Process Reward Models (PRMs) that provide step-level supervision for LLM reasoning. The key innovation is formulating PRM training as a two-player, general-sum game between a generator and a reward model. Empirically, APRM outperforms strong baselines across multiple mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks.

strengths.value:
1. The paper identifies a clear limitation in existing PRM training (static data, poor generalization) and proposes an elegant, game-theoretic solution. The adversarial setup for generating an adaptive curriculum of hard negatives is a conceptually compelling idea.

2. The method is evaluated thoroughly across diverse benchmarks and model families. The results are consistently strong, demonstrating not just better accuracy but also properties like robustness, scalability, and cross-domain generalization.

weaknesses.value:
1. The adversarial training process, involving two models trained with a combination of PPO and OGDA, is inherently more computationally expensive and complex than normal PRM training.

2. The step level oracles introduced in the paper are sophisticated but imperfect automated validators that enables scalable training without human annotation, but also introduces dependence on its rule completeness and accuracy.

3. A significant gap is the lack of comparison with a baseline that directly performs RL on the solver using the same automated oracle for improved reasoning. This makes it difficult to isolate the contribution of the complex adversarial game from the mere availability of automated step-level supervision using PPO. Also see Q1.

questions.value: The proposed method already contains PPO on the solver model. Why not use direct RL to improve LLM reasoning using the step level rule based reward and the final correctness reward? Does it introduce reward hacking?

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission9885 by Reviewer nTz3

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful review, and for recognizing the novelty of our game-theoretic framework for PRM training and strong empirical performance of our approach. We are grateful for the insightful questions raised and answer them below.

> W1: The adversarial training process, involving two models trained with a combination of PPO and OGDA, is inherently more computationally expensive and complex than normal PRM training.

We agree that $\texttt{APRM}$ is slightly computationally expensive because it involves training two models using RL (generator and PRM). But this cost is incurred only during training, the test-time cost is identical to the data-driven techniques. In practice the **total training cost is modest** (as discussed in Figure 3, Appendix 6.9): $\texttt{APRM}$ requires 72 GPU hours, which is only 1.25x that of ReST-MCTS (60 GPU hours). This is far less compared to prior adversarial approaches such as [1] which  train three models, increasing the training cost by 3x. Thus, although our method is more expensive than static data-driven PRMs, the added computational burden is limited and yields stronger PRMs.

---

> W2: The step-level oracles introduced in the paper are sophisticated but imperfect automated validators that enables scalable training without human annotation, but also introduces dependence on its rule completeness and accuracy.

Thank you for raising this concern. We acknowledge that the term “oracle’’ may be misleading and will replace it with the more accurate term **“rule-based proximity check’’** in the revised paper.

The rule-based proximity check is **not a correctness evaluator**. It does not determine whether a step is mathematically valid in isolation, nor does it attempt to judge step-level correctness for each question. Its purpose is solely to act as a **conservative filter**: if a generated step is trivially equivalent to the gold step—symbolically or semantically—it is discarded from the training process rather than mislabeled as a negative. Because the check operates by comparing a candidate step to the gold, it is **question-agnostic** and its completeness is not central to the functioning of $\texttt{APRM}$.

---

> Q1(a): The proposed method already contains PPO on the solver model. 

We would like to clarify that we **do not train the Solver model** in our approach. Our method involves three models: the **generator**, the **process reward model (PRM)**, and the **solver**.

Importantly, the **solver remains completely static** throughout. We do **not** finetune the solver with PPO or any other RL algorithm. The training proceeds in two phases:

1. PRM Training: Generator and PRM are trained in tandem, solver is not used in this phase 
2. Evaluation: we then use the trained PRM to guide the frozen solver at test time, rejecting the incorrect steps and regenerating them. This is a test-time scaling technique, not RL training of the solver.

title.value: Continued response to the reviewer nTz3

comment.value:
> W3 and Q1 (b): A significant gap is the lack of comparison with a baseline that directly performs RL on the solver using the same automated oracle for improved reasoning. This makes it difficult to isolate the contribution of the complex adversarial game from the mere availability of automated step-level supervision using PPO. Why not use direct RL to improve LLM reasoning using the step level rule based reward and the final correctness reward?

As described in response to W2, the rule-based proximity check cannot provide stand-alone dense supervision. It only _checks whether a generated perturbation of the gold step is too similar to the gold_; it does **not** evaluate correctness for arbitrary solver-generated steps.

_Why it is not possible to train solver using rule based reward?_

In solver training, the sampled steps are typically **not** perturbations of the corresponding gold step, rather a problem can be solved in many ways. Consequently, the proximity check would **provide random or misleading signals**. Incorrect steps that coincidentally pass the filter would be marked as “correct”. This would be **discarded during PRM training but reinforced during solver RL training**, harming performance.

To illustrate this limitation, consider:

- Question: “A pool doubles every hour; how large after five hours?”
- Correct step: “Double after one hour; four times after two hours.”
- Incorrect step: “Double after one hour; three times after two hours.”

The incorrect step passes the proximity filters and since the expressions are not symbolically comparable, the incorrect step would be mistakenly labeled as correct. In **PRM training, such cases are discarded and do not harm learning**; but in solver RL, they would reinforce incorrect behavior.

Nevertheless, we performed the requested RL experiment. We finetune Gemma-3-12B using: (a) final correctness reward, (b) rule-based reward + final correctness (requested experiment), and (c) dense rewards from an APRM-trained PRM. All models are trained on the MATH training split.

| Method              | MATH500 | JEEB | OlympiadB | AIME25 | AMC  |
|---------------------|--------:|-----:|----------:|-------:|-----:|
| Base Model (CoT)    |   76.8  | 43.2 |   35.6    | 53.0   | 23.3 |
| Final Correct  Reward     |   80.0  | 48.2 |   40.0    | 59.8   | 21.0 |
| Rule Based Reward | 78.5 | 46.9 | 38.7 | 58.1 | 20.5 |
| **APRM (Ours)**     | **86.8** | **58.6** | **48.0** | **65.7** | **25.3** |

We observe that using the rule-based check as a reward harms solver RL performance relative to final correctness alone (**–1.5pp** on MATH500, **–1.3pp** on JEEB, **–1.3pp** on AIME25). In contrast, the dense reward from an APRM-trained PRM provides a strong and reliable supervision signal, yielding **+6.8pp** (MATH500), **+10.4pp** (JEEB), **+10.9pp** (AIME25), and **+4.3pp** (AMC) over final-answer-based RL, this demonstrates APRMs advantage for RL post-training.

---

> Q1 (c) : Does it introduce reward hacking?

Yes, direct RL with the rule-based proximity signal would be vulnerable to reward hacking, because the signal does not measure correctness. An example is discussed in response to W3/Q1(b) where the trained model would generate incorrect steps that are trivial perturbations of the correct step because those steps are positively reinforced by the rule based reward. 

---

We thank the reviewer again for these helpful suggestions. We believe the revised clarifications and additional experiments address the concerns. If there are any concerns that need further clarification, we would be happy to address them. 

We look forward to your response.

summary.value: This paper proposes Adversarially Trained Process Reward Models (APRM), a framework that treats PRM training as a two-player general-sum game between (i) a generator that tries to produce plausible but wrong reasoning steps, and (ii) a process reward model that tries to detect those subtle errors. By letting the generator constantly generate harder negatives, the PRM is exposed to an adaptive curriculum rather than a fixed, static dataset, which the paper argues is the core weakness of current PRM training.

strengths.value:
1. The general-sum + Nash existence via Glicksberg is reasonable for the PRM and generator adversarial setup case.
2. The inclusion of OGDA and regularization terms is justified with references to convergence theory.
3. The evaluations cover multiple domains, datasets, and solvers, with consistent gains across both in-domain and out-of-distribution tasks.

weaknesses.value:
1. When summarizing synthetic data generation techniques, the authors miss works, MM-PRM, FG-PRM, and FreePRM.
2. Maintaining two RL-trained LLMs (generator + PRM) is computationally expensive and less accessible than data-driven PRMs.
3. APRM still struggles with certain logic or precondition-based reasoning failures that are difficult to model via token-level perturbations.

questions.value:
1. What mechanisms ensure that the generator explores fundamentally different reasoning errors rather than minor textual perturbations?
2. Would a simpler hard-negative mining approach from failed solver traces achieve similar benefits without full adversarial RL? In other words, how much of the +3.4 pp is from adversariality instead of fresh and more complex data?

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission9885 by Reviewer Y618

comment.value:
We thank the reviewers for recognizing the theoretically grounded algorithms presented in this work and are grateful for the insightful comments. Please find the answers to the questions and concerns below.

> W1: The authors miss works, MM-PRM, FG-PRM, and FreePRM.

We thank the reviewer for pointing out these relevant works. We have added MM-PRM, FG-PRM, and FreePRM to the related-work section in our paper.

While these approaches rely on synthetically generated data from a static model for PRM training, APRM uses an adversarial framework to generate progressively harder training data from an evolving generator.

---

> W2: Maintaining two RL-trained LLMs (generator + PRM) is computationally expensive and less accessible than data-driven PRMs.

We agree that $\texttt{APRM}$ is computationally expensive, but this cost is incurred once only during training, the test-time cost is identical to the data-driven techniques. In practice the total training cost is modest (as discussed in Figure 3, Appendix 6.9): APRM requires 72 GPU hours, which is only 1.2x that of ReST-MCTS (60 GPU hours). This is far less compared to prior adversarial approaches, such as [1], that trains three models, increasing the training cost by 3x. 

---

> W3:  APRM still struggles with certain logic or precondition-based reasoning failures that are difficult to model via token-level perturbations.

We agree that APRM struggles with precondition-based errors, we discuss these in Appendix 6.6. These cases are challenging for all existing PRM approaches. APRM still provides consistent improvements over prior methods on other failure modes, Appendix 6.4 includes examples where APRM successfully identifies errors that other methods miss.

We hypothesize, this could be a limitation of the generator size rather than a fundamental limitation of APRM. As shown in Fig. 2, increasing the generator size (while keeping the PRM fixed) yields an additional +3% improvement, suggesting that a larger generator exposes the PRM to a broader range of failure modes. We expect that continuing to scale the generator would further reduce these remaining weaknesses.

---

> Q1: Mechanisms to ensure the generator explores distinct reasoning errors: 

We structure the proposed two-player game so that only non-trivial perturbations that evade the current PRM yield positive reward for the generator, and everything else is either discarded or negatively reinforced. There are three mechanisms to avoid the generator from generating trivial paraphrases of the gold solution and exploring fundamentally different reasoning errors. 

-  _Step-level Rule-Based checks_: Steps that are too similar to the gold response (e.g. minor textual perturbations), and steps that yield the same result after symbolic computation are filtered by the step-level oracle and are not used during training. 
- _Adversarial training_: Early in training, generator(G) may produce trivial errors. The PRM is trained on these errors, and once the PRM detects such patterns, the generator receives a non-positive reward for generating them (Eq. 3). If PRM has not seen a trivial pattern before, it learns it; thereafter, such perturbations no longer yield reward to the generator. Only non-trivial, PRM-evading perturbations are incentivized via a positive reward. This forces the generator to discover new errors that lie beyond PRM’s current detection capabilities. 
- _Replay Buffer_: The PRM may forget easier errors as training progresses and might reward generator for trivial errors. To avoid forgetting previously encountered error modes, we maintain a replay buffer of past errors generated by the generator and use them with the new errors during PRM’s training. This establishes that previously covered trivial errors remain detectable and therefore non-rewarding for the generator across training.

_Experimental evidence_. We also show qualitatively and qualitatively that the generator progresses to explore fundamental reasoning errors. 
1. The qualitative trajectory reported in Appendix 6.2 shows the generator’s evolution from shallow mistakes (e.g., miscounts) to locally consistent but globally misconstrued steps, and eventually to conceptual errors (e.g., unweighted vs. weighted averaging of probabilities). 

2. Appendix 6.3 further shows that the PRM remains effective when the mistakes become more subtle to identify, showing that it encountered such subtler mistakes during its training. 

3. Cross-domain results on SciBench (Table 2 and Appendix 6.5) indicate that generator perturbations capture domain-agnostic error structures (e.g., unit conversion, some precondition violations), consistent with non-trivial perturbations rather than surface paraphrases.

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer Y618

comment.value:
> Q2: Would a simpler hard-negative mining approach from failed solver traces achieve similar benefits without full adversarial RL?  In other words, how much of the +3.4 pp is from adversariality instead of fresh and more complex data?

We thank the reviewer for this suggestion and ran the requested hard-negative baseline.

We train a PRM on hard negatives mined from static ReST-MCTS solver traces. ReST-MCTS runs MCTS over reasoning steps and assigns a value $v_k \in [0,1]$ to each partial solution. To extract hard negatives, we select 
1. step-level errors that do not lie on any correct trace but have high $v_k$
2. “near-miss’’ nodes whose siblings lie on correct reasoning paths. 

We then train a PRM on these mined negatives plus the corresponding positive steps. The results are shown in the table below. 


| Method           | MATH500 | JEEBench | OlympiadB | AIME25 | AMC  |
|------------------|-------:|-------:|-------------:|--------:|------:|
| |       |         **GPT-OSS-120B**     |    |        |      |
| Hard Neg.        | 91.2    | 69.5 | 79.2      | 91.5   | 68.5 |
| ReST-MCTS        | 91.6    | 69.1 | 84.3      | 91.0   | 67.4 |
| APRM (Ours)      | 91.4    | 70.3 | 89.4      | 94.5   | 70.7 |
| ||**Gemma-3-27B**  |       |         |      |
| Hard Neg.        | 86.0    | 63.0 | 83.0      | 89.1   | 60.0 |
| ReST-MCTS        | 93.2    | 70.3 | 84.3      | 90.6   | 61.2 |
| APRM (Ours)      | 91.4    | 74.4 | 90.7      | 91.9   | 60.8 |

**Results.**
APRM outperforms Hard Negative mining by **+3.2 pp** (GPT-OSS-120B) and **+5.6 pp** (Gemma-3-27B).
Hard Neg. performs worse than training on all ReST-MCTS trajectories by **−0.7 pp** and **−3.7 pp**, respectively.

These results show that while hard negatives are beneficial, they are not sufficient on their own. PRM training benefits from a diversity of errors including simpler errors. Restricting training only to difficult mistakes leads to forgetting of simpler errors. APRM avoids this issue by maintaining a buffer of past generator errors (see Sec 3.1).

---

_Why hard negative from a static solver does not suffice?_

 Any fixed solver has inherent limits on the types of mistakes it can produce. Once the solver has exhausted those failure modes, it becomes increasingly difficult to obtain new or more complex negative data. We address this challenge in our work. Generating fresh, harder errors requires an evolving generator—not a static model—because the space of mistakes reachable by a static model is inherently restricted. 

Our experiments (Section 3, Table 1) show that guiding the solver using APRM trained PRM consistently outperforms ReST-MCTS trained PRM which relies on failed solver traces from a single static model.

---

We thank the reviewer again for the detailed feedback and constructive suggestions. We believe the revisions and additional experiments have addressed all raised concerns, but if anything remains unresolved, we would be happy to clarify further. 

We appreciate your time and look forward to your response.

Key Concern: Asked to cite and compare against a baseline ("ARM" - Adversarial Training of Reward Models) and requested evaluation of the PRM for RL post-training (not just inference verification).


Our Response:

New Baseline (ARM): We implemented the ARM baseline. **APRM outperformed it significantly, +7.2 pp** on GPT-OSS-120B. 

New Experiment (RL Post-Training): We used the APRM-trained PRM to train a solver (using GRPO). It outperforms both the ReST-MCTS baseline (by **+3.8pp**) and standard outcome-based RL (**+6.8pp**).


The reviewer explicitly stated their **assessment shifted from 4 to 6 following the rebuttal**


---

Both the reviewers nTz3 and Y618 had concern regarding the training costs of APRM.

One response: We clarified that training cost is only 1.2x that of standard methods (72 vs. 60 GPU hours), not prohibitively expensive

---


We believe these additional experiments establish the necessity and effectiveness of APRM against all suggested baselines.
